text.p: Marxist guerrillas released another 20 hostages from the residence of the Japanese ambassador in Lima on Saturday, keeping 83 captives in the mined and booby-trapped building they seized in a spectacular assault 11 days ago.

Saturday's release followed the first face-to-face talks between the guerrillas and the government negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, appointed by President Alberto Fujimori to help solve the hostage crisis.

Palermo said in a brief statement that the talks, which lasted three hours and 15 minutes, had "produced advances for the solution of this serious incident ... We achieved liberating 20 hostages and those who remain are in good health."

Dressed in the crumpled but elegant suits they wore to a reception on December 17 to mark the birthday of Japanese Emperor Akihito, the freed hostages walked out of the building in single file and boarded a blue-and-white bus that took them to Lima's police hospital for a checkup.

Since guerrillas of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the residence, they have released more than 420 of their hostages -- without apparent concessions from Fujimori. He has flatly rejected guerrilla demands to free 400 guerrillas from Peruvian jails.
Three hostages were freed initially: the ambassador of the Dominican Republic, Jose Diaz, the Malaysian ambassador, Ahmad Mokhtar, and a prominent Peruvian businessman, Enrique Pendavis.

The three walked from the residence to a cluster of reporters in the street. Pendavis then read out a communique from the guerrillas in which they objected to being labeled terrorists and angrily rejected comparisons between the Tupac Amaru and the Shining Path, Peru's older and more violent guerrilla group.
"We deplore that we are being called a band of terrorists," the communique said. "This is absolutely false."
They then returned to the threshold of the residence and were joined by the other 17 captives, who together stepped to freedom.

Since winning elections in 1990, Fujimori cracked down on both the Shining Path and Tupac Amaru, with his army pursuing them into remote jungle and mountain strongholds and taking hundreds of prisoner.
Until the December 17 raid on the Japanese residence, Fujimori had claimed to have restored peace and tranquility to Peru after years of guerrilla raids and bomb attacks.

The hostages released on Saturday included several representatives of major companies from Japan, which had become the biggest donor of development aid to Peru since Fujimori took power. The president is of Japanese origin.

Fujimori's uncompromising stand on the guerrillas' demands won solid backing from home and abroad on Friday, when the Group of Seven (G7) industrial nations issued a strongly worded communique condemning the rebels as "terrorists."
The G7 statement promised to help the Peruvian government with "all the appropriate means that it could request."
Shortly afterwards, the Peruvian Congress voted -- 82 to 0, with eight abstentions -- to give "full support to the government and (whatever) decisions it takes to solve this grave crisis."
The hostages still held include high-ranking Peruvian police and government officials, who are considered useful pawns in the Tupa Amaru's high-stakes game of chess with the government.
The 20-odd guerrilla group holding the residence is led by Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, a veteran leftist militant with a record of violent actions.
Shortly before government negotiator Palermo entered the residence on Saturday, police doubled their security cordon around the building, which takes up almost an entire block.
On Friday, police arrested three suspected guerrillas -- two women and a man -- who posed as street vendors outside the residence.
The latest development in the hostage crisis came against the background of hardline statements from both sides which had given little reason for hope that a breakthrough might be near.

In the latest of several media appearances by guerrilla spokesmen whose authenticity is far from certain, a hooded man identifying himself as Commandante Santana said in a television interview from New York on Friday that the residence would be blown up on New Year's day unless Fujimori agreed to their demands.
"We will execute all the hostages on January 1," he said, unless the government bowed to their demands.
Japan, whose nationals account for the largest number of hostages after Peru, stressed on Saturday that the crisis must be ended without loss of life.

"There is little advantage in reaching a compromise with terrorists, but a peaceful solution has become the key word in terms of preserving the lives of the captives," Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters during his regular daily call at a crisis room in the Foreign Ministry.
